newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RUGBY UNION - Springbok coach still learning the ropes.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION - Springbok coach still learning the ropes.

text.p: WELLINGTON, July 14 - Carel du Plessis may have soothed the national stress and perhaps extended his Springboks coaching career just a wee bit, but as with most South African fans you can't take the confidence out of his rugby.

Du Plessis just managed to hang on to his short career as the South African coach when the Springboks avoided a humiliating whitewash by the British Lions by winning the dead-rubber third test last week.
After losing the series, their third and final test victory came as a welcome relief for every South African fan, du Plessis included.
"Yes, there was a lot of pressure. But that third test just reflected on the whole series. We should have won 3-0," the former Springboks winger said.
South Africans are immensely proud of their rugby, just like New Zealanders. The difference is that their pride oozes confidence, sometimes bordering on arrogance, which make them fierce competitors.
The All Blacks put them in their rightful place by winning the '96 series, in all winning three tests out of four.

A year later the British Lions presented them with a second consecutive beating and like in the '96 series, the meaningless final test was "given" away to the South Africans which perhaps prevented a national disaster.
"We scored three tries in the second test, they didn't cross our line -- so that should say plenty about the series," du Plessis argued.
All Black coach John Hart thought the Springboks should have won the second test, and maybe all three of them.
But, Hart has developed a habit of lifting the opposition to the highest level possible with words before meeting them on the field. Fiji and Argentina were no different.
But the rich history of rugby rivalry between New Zealand and South Africa has it that no victory has been easily achieved.
The opening Tri-series test at Ellis Park between the two teams next Sunday (NZ time) will be the All Blacks' toughest match this season.

Hart believes the following week's test against Australia in Melbourne will be just as tough given the amount of travelling involved between the games and extreme conditions between the two countries.
"If we came up with one win away from home I'll be happy. We'll have the chance of defending the tri-series," Hart said.
The high veldt conditions at Ellis Park have had much to do with the Springboks' undefeated run at the venue since 1993.

Du Plessis, who weathered a hostile call from the rugby public to resign after the Springboks' second test loss to the Lions, last week ducked away with a few senior players to analyse their three tests against the Lions and work on a few strategies for the All Black test.
He was reluctant to disclose who the midweek think-tank included but admitted that he was always going to reassess the Springboks' game and re-launch their plans to tackle the Tri-series.
"The first leg of the season (Lions series) is over. The next is the Tri-series and it's normal for any coach to make some assessments and adjustments," he said.

Du Plessis had sung a wide-ranging game for the Springboks this season but after the first test loss to the Lions, he seemed to have reverted to the old Springboks strengths -- starting with a ferocious forward game.
He picked a massive pack, where mobility and all-round skills had given way to muscles and aggression.
Du Plessis said the South African rugby public was unforgiving.
"After the World Cup win everyone seems to be taking losses here harder.

"If I was talking to South African reporters I'd be asking them to be constructive in their criticisms. When a new coach comes in, he wants to start rebuilding in his own style. If you expect instant success, that's not fair.
"We've got 13 tests this year and you ask yourself for the sake of the fans: 'Is there room for mistakes?'."

Du Plessis, who made his Springboks' debut on the tour of New Zealand in 1981, played 12 tests for his country until 1989. He missed the test matches and made his first full international appearance the following year against the Jaguars, a South American team made up mostly of Argentinian test players.

In all he played 22 matches for the Springboks and his appearances were restricted by South Africa's isolation then. He still holds the Currie Cup record for the highest number of tries in a season -- 19.
His total of 51 Currie Cup tries was a record until just recently and underscored his brilliant playing career.
At 38, he is the youngest coach of a major playing test-playing nation, and admits he is still coming to grips with coaching.
